title: The English Verb System
orientation: The English verb system is a set of connected patterns, not a list of tense names. A verb’s form helps build its phrase, while its lexical meaning influences the complements it permits. Today develops both aspects. You will learn the principal forms, distinguish lexical verbs from auxiliaries and construct ordinary questions and negatives. You will then compare objects with predicative complements and examine why one verb may allow a pattern that another does not. These foundations support the tense, aspect, modality, voice and non-finite lessons that follow. Do not expect to master every later distinction today. First learn to explain a short verb phrase and identify its surrounding participants. The advanced layers clarify finite status, auxiliary order, stative interpretations and ergative alternations, giving you a reliable way to analyse unfamiliar examples without calling every subject a doer or every -ed form past tense.
outcomes: Identify principal forms, auxiliary uses and finite/non-finite status in taught patterns.
Construct ordinary questions and negatives with appropriate inversion or do-support.
Distinguish direct objects, indirect objects, predicative complements and selected locative complements.
Explain lexical valency restrictions rather than convert every verb mechanically.
Distinguish stative/dynamic senses and active ergative alternations from passive voice.

modules.title: Lexical verbs, auxiliaries and the principal forms
modules.definition: Verbs are a word class whose members organise clauses and select characteristic patterns. Lexical verbs contribute central meanings such as wait, repair and know. Auxiliaries help express grammatical meanings and constructions. Finite and non-finite describe a verb form’s grammatical status within a clause, not whether it denotes an action.
foundation: Learn a lexical verb through its principal forms. Write has the plain form write, third-person singular present writes, past wrote, past participle written and -ing form writing. A regular verb normally uses the same -ed form for its past and past participle: repair, repaired, repaired. An irregular verb has an established alternative pattern, as write/wrote/written or cut/cut/cut. Identical spelling can therefore serve different grammatical roles. The clause She cut the paper contains a past form, while has cut contains a past participle selected by has. A learner’s dictionary supplies the relevant forms and pronunciation.
intermediate: Be, have and do are primary verbs that can function as auxiliaries or lexical verbs. Compare She has a bicycle with She has repaired a bicycle; only the second has is a perfect auxiliary. Be forms include be, am, is, are, was, were, been and being. Have has the forms have, has, had and having; do has do, does, did, done and doing. Had serves as both past and past-participle form. Core modal auxiliaries include can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would and must. They normally select a plain verb form: can swim, not can swims. Modality receives fuller semantic treatment on Day 17.
advanced: In a finite verb phrase, the first verb is finite and the following forms are selected by preceding auxiliaries: has written, is writing, may have written. Non-finite forms include to-infinitives, plain infinitives, -ing forms and past participles. The form after to in to write does not carry its own person agreement. A past participle is not a past-tense verb merely because its name contains past; The work will be finished refers forward in time. Finite does not mean that a form always visibly changes for every subject: modal can has the same spelling with I and she.
expert: Inflectional form, clause status and time reference are different dimensions. A plain form occurs in several environments, including after a modal and in an imperative such as Close the door. Modern descriptions differ in how they classify certain untensed or subjunctive constructions, so a visible -s or -ed ending cannot serve as the sole test for finiteness. Regular spelling also has conditions: stopped doubles a consonant, while opened does not; consult stress and spelling conventions rather than double every final consonant. British learnt/learned and American learned illustrate legitimate form variation, not an automatic difference in grammatical correctness.

patterns.form: lexical verb: plain / -s / past / past participle / -ing
patterns.meaning: write / writes / wrote / written / writing are the five principal form categories.
Can write uses a plain form after the modal.

examples.analysis: Writes is the third-person singular present form of the lexical verb.

examples.sentence: The researcher has written three reports.

examples.sentence: The researcher may have been working late.

contrasts.b: She has opened a small studio.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. Has is lexical possession in the first and a perfect auxiliary in the second.

exceptions: A form can be irregular without changing its spelling across categories: cut serves as plain, past and past participle in different structures. Context and auxiliary selection distinguish the functions.

mistakes.reason: Perfect have requires the past participle, not the past-simple form wrote.
A core modal normally selects the plain form, not the third-person singular form.

glossary.definition: A verb with grammatical functions such as forming perfect, progressive, passive, modal, interrogative or negative constructions.
glossary.example: Has is auxiliary in has arrived.

glossary.example: Has is finite in she has arrived.

modules.title: Verb-phrase order, do-support, questions and negation
modules.definition: A verb phrase can contain a lexical verb with one or more auxiliaries. English auxiliaries have an ordered relationship and select the form of the next verb. Do-support supplies auxiliary do where a neutral question or negative needs an auxiliary and no suitable one is already present.
foundation: Begin with an existing auxiliary. She is working becomes Is she working? and She is not working. The finite auxiliary moves before the subject in this yes–no question, and not follows that auxiliary in the negative. With a modal, the same basic pattern gives Can she swim? and She cannot swim. The lexical verb does not move to the front by itself in an ordinary present-day neutral question. Be can also invert directly when it links a subject with a description: Is she ready? Do not automatically add do simply because there is only one written verb.
intermediate: For an ordinary lexical verb without another auxiliary, use do, does or did: Do they work here? Does she work here? Did she work here? The lexical verb returns to its plain form because the auxiliary carries the relevant finite contrast. Negatives follow the same arrangement: They do not work here; she did not work here. Do can occur both as auxiliary and lexical verb: Do they do laboratory work? A neutral affirmative subject question ordinarily needs no added do: Who wrote the report? Object questions do use it when needed: Who did they invite? Emphatic contexts can produce different patterns.
advanced: The common auxiliary order is modal, perfect have, progressive be, passive be and lexical verb. Each item selects what immediately follows: have selects a past participle; progressive be selects an -ing form; passive be selects a past participle. Thus may have been waiting is interpretable through nested selections rather than a memorised label alone. Longer combinations can be grammatical but cumbersome, so choose a simpler wording where it preserves meaning. Questions invert the first finite auxiliary only: Has she been waiting? Negation normally follows that same first auxiliary.
expert: Contractions join forms in writing and speech: is not/isn’t, do not/don’t, I am/I’m and they have/they’ve. Their suitability depends on register, audience and emphasis; formal writing does not have one universal grammatical ban on them. The spelling ’s can mean is or has, and ’d can mean had or would; the surrounding pattern resolves ambiguity where possible. Auxiliary and lexical have show regional and constructional variation, including Have you got a pen? and Do you have a pen? Neutral be normally avoids do-support in finite questions, but imperatives such as Do be careful and Don’t be late show that do and be are not universally incompatible.

patterns.form: finite auxiliary + subject + remaining verb phrase
patterns.meaning: Has she been waiting? inverts only the first finite auxiliary.
Did the learners finish? uses did, leaving finish plain.

examples.analysis: Does carries the present third-person contrast; repair remains plain.

examples.sentence: The visitors have not been waiting long.
examples.analysis: Not follows finite have; been and waiting retain the selected forms.

examples.sentence: Do be patient while the file loads.
examples.analysis: Emphatic imperative do can occur with be; this is a special construction, not an ordinary neutral yes–no question.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. Who is subject in the first and object in the second, so the ordinary question structures differ.

exceptions: Do is not added mechanically to every question. A neutral subject question such as Who arrived? and a be-question such as Are they ready? already have their appropriate structures.

mistakes.problem: Did she went to the archive?
mistakes.repair: Did she go to the archive?
mistakes.reason: Did carries the finite past contrast; the following lexical verb is plain.

mistakes.problem: Does she is ready? Intended: a neutral present question.
mistakes.reason: Ordinary finite be inverts without do-support in this question.

glossary.definition: Use of auxiliary do in constructions such as relevant questions, negatives or emphasis.
A reversal of normal subject–auxiliary order in the relevant construction.
glossary.example: She has arrived becomes Has she arrived?

modules.title: Valency, objects, predicative complements and sentence patterns
modules.definition: Verb valency concerns the participants and complement patterns associated with a verb use. Transitive uses have an object; intransitive uses do not. Linking and complex-transitive patterns contain predicative complements that describe a subject or object rather than introduce another independent participant.
foundation: Compare The child laughed with The child opened the box. Laughed is intransitive here; opened is transitive and has the box as direct object. This is a grammatical pattern distinction, not simply a distinction between physical actions and states. She owns a bicycle contains a direct object even though owning is not a momentary action. Conversely, The glass broke has a subject undergoing a change without a direct object. Identify grammatical function from the structure and the particular verb use. Some verbs allow more than one pattern: She is reading and She is reading a novel are both possible.
intermediate: A ditransitive pattern contains two objects: The tutor gave the learner a booklet. The learner is the indirect object and a booklet the direct object. In The tutor gave a booklet to the learner, this course calls to the learner a prepositional complement rather than a second noun-phrase object. Some traditional accounts extend indirect object more broadly, so compare the stated analysis before treating a terminology difference as a grammatical fault. A linking pattern relates a subject to a description or identity: The learner seemed tired; Leena became a doctor. Tired and a doctor are predicative complements.
advanced: Complex-transitive patterns add a complement describing the object: The panel considered the plan practical; They appointed Leena coordinator. The second complement is not an indirect object receiving a separate thing. Other verbs require a location complement: Put the folder on the shelf. On the shelf completes the placement pattern; merely saying Put the folder normally leaves the instruction incomplete. Complements can therefore be noun phrases, adjective phrases, prepositional phrases or clauses, depending on the verb. Optional adjuncts add circumstances: She read the report yesterday. Distinguishing optionality from the verb’s meaning requirements needs more than a single deletion test.
expert: The verb’s lexical meaning and construction jointly determine which pattern is available. Explain normally takes a content object with a to-phrase for the listener: explain the rule to me, not explain me the rule in the broad edited standard used here. Tell allows tell me the rule, illustrating a genuine lexical difference rather than a universal conversion rule between two-object and prepositional patterns. Valency counts may include the subject as an argument in linguistic descriptions; a classroom list of objects often counts something different. Day 13 develops hierarchical parsing and diagnostic tests. Avoid defining every object as a person physically receiving an action or every complement as an adjective after be.

patterns.form: S + V; S + V + O; S + V + subject complement
patterns.meaning: The guests laughed; the guests opened the gate; the guests seemed tired.

patterns.form: S + V + indirect object + direct object; S + V + object + object complement
patterns.meaning: She gave him a key; they painted the gate blue.

examples.sentence: The lecturer sent the students a reading list.
examples.analysis: The students and a reading list are the two noun-phrase objects in this use.

examples.sentence: The committee found the explanation unconvincing.
examples.analysis: Explanation is object; unconvincing is a complement describing it, not an adverb modifying found.

examples.sentence: Please put the parcel beside the desk.
examples.analysis: The placement verb selects a locative complement; beside the desk states the required destination.

contrasts.a: The tutor gave Lina a booklet.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first has two objects; the second has an object plus a description of that object.

exceptions: The same lexical verb can have transitive and intransitive uses. She is eating does not become ungrammatical merely because eat can also take an object in She is eating an apple.

mistakes.problem: Please explain me the procedure. Broad edited standard requested.
mistakes.repair: Please explain the procedure to me.
mistakes.reason: Explain and tell do not share every complement pattern.

mistakes.problem: Intended: the plan was impractical. They judged the plan impractically.
mistakes.reason: For the stated judgement about the plan, impractical is a predicative adjective describing the object. Impractically could instead describe a manner of judging in a different context, which is not the intended meaning here.

glossary.definition: The argument and complement pattern associated with a lexical use, with counting conventions stated by the analysis.
glossary.example: Give can occur with giver, recipient and thing given.

glossary.definition: An expression describing or identifying a subject or object.

modules.title: Alternations, dynamic meanings and states
modules.definition: Dynamic meanings present events, activities or changes; stative meanings present situations such as knowledge or possession without an internal activity sequence. An ergative alternation relates a transitive use with an intransitive use in which the affected object becomes the subject, as The wind opened the door and The door opened. Its intransitive partner is active, rather than a passive construction.
foundation: A dynamic use can involve a deliberate action, such as writing a note, or an uncontrolled event, such as a branch falling. A stative use describes a situation such as knowing the answer, owning a bicycle or resembling a parent. This distinction concerns how a meaning is presented, not whether the real world changes over a lifetime. A person can own a bicycle only temporarily, but ownership can still be described as a state. Begin by interpreting the particular sentence rather than assigning an unchanging dynamic or stative label to the dictionary spelling.
intermediate: Several verbs have different senses with different patterns. I think the plan is useful states an opinion; I am thinking about the plan presents mental activity. She has a bicycle expresses possession; she is having lunch describes an activity. The soup tastes salty describes its perceived quality; the cook is tasting the soup describes an action. Progressive forms are more typical of dynamic uses, but the relationship is not an absolute prohibition. A speaker can present temporary behaviour with be: He is being unusually quiet. Future lessons develop the semantic choices among simple, progressive and perfect constructions.
advanced: In an ergative alternation, the affected participant appears as object in one clause and subject in another: The heat melted the wax; the wax melted. The second clause is active intransitive, not passive: it has no passive be plus participle construction. The subject need not be a conscious doer, so defining every subject as the actor produces a false analysis. Not all transitive verbs permit this alternation: The courier delivered the parcel does not yield The parcel delivered with the ordinary completed-delivery meaning. Whether an alternation is available is a lexical and constructional fact to learn.
expert: Progressive stative uses can be marked by register, temporary construal or evolving convention. I’m loving the new course is common informal evaluative English; that does not license an ordinary factual I’m knowing the answer in every context. Conversely, a temporary context can make a progressive natural with a verb otherwise often labelled stative, as The repairs are costing more than expected. Ergative is also used in wider linguistic typology for case and alignment systems. The English teaching label here refers only to the illustrated causative/inchoative alternation; it does not claim that English has a general ergative case system. Day 19 revisits alternation alongside voice.

patterns.form: causing subject + transitive verb + affected object ↔ affected subject + intransitive verb
patterns.meaning: The wind opened the gate ↔ The gate opened.

patterns.form: same spelling + different lexical sense → different aspect possibilities
patterns.meaning: Think as opinion contrasts with think as ongoing consideration.

examples.sentence: The falling branch broke the window. The window broke.
examples.analysis: The affected window is object in the transitive use and subject in the intransitive use.

examples.sentence: She has two bicycles, but she is having lunch now.
examples.analysis: Possession and eating lunch are different senses of have.

examples.sentence: The repairs are costing the club more than expected.
examples.analysis: The progressive presents an ongoing developing financial consequence; a blanket stative ban would be misleading.

contrasts.note: Both are active clauses. The second leaves the cause unstated through an intransitive alternation rather than a passive transformation.

exceptions: A lexical spelling does not fix one aspect class across all senses. The cook is tasting the sauce is an ordinary dynamic use even though The sauce tastes sweet describes a state.

mistakes.problem: For the ordinary knowledge-state meaning: I am knowing the answer.
mistakes.reason: The simple form is the normal neutral expression of this knowledge state.

mistakes.problem: Intended ordinary delivery meaning: The parcel delivered at noon.
mistakes.repair: The courier delivered the parcel at noon.
mistakes.reason: Deliver does not permit this intended subject alternation merely because some change-of-state verbs do; a passive with was delivered is another possible structure.

glossary.definition: A situation construed as a state rather than an unfolding activity or event.
A transitive/intransitive pairing in which the transitive object corresponds to the intransitive subject.
glossary.example: The heat melted the ice; the ice melted.

questions.prompt: Which is the past participle of write?

An indirect object receiving the plan.
A second direct object naming another entity.

questions.prompt: Which analysis fits The wax melted?
options: A passive requiring an omitted was.
A clause with wax as direct object.
A sentence without a grammatical subject.
An active intransitive clause with wax as affected subject.
questions.why: The verb occurs in its intransitive alternation; no passive be-participle construction is present.

questions.prompt: Why is The cook is tasting the soup ordinary?

Every sense of taste must use the progressive.
An object always makes a verb stative.
Progressive be can only precede a noun.

writing.prompt: Write 80–110 words about a workplace or class activity. Include an intransitive verb, a direct object, a two-object pattern, a subject complement, an object complement and a question or negative with do-support. Identify the patterns afterwards.
writing.model:
The workshop began at nine. The tutor gave each participant a short checklist and explained the safety rules to the group. Everyone examined a damaged bicycle before the demonstration, checking the frame as well as the wheels. The brakes seemed unreliable, and the tutor considered the repair urgent. Did the group understand the first procedure? The tutor repeated it carefully, then waited while the learners checked their own equipment. Nobody rushed to replace a part before identifying the problem. At the end, the participants compared their findings and asked further questions.

Analysis: Began and waited are intransitive here; examined has a direct object. Gave each participant a short checklist has two objects. Unreliable is subject complement; urgent is object complement. Did…understand uses do-support.
rubric: Use each required pattern with an appropriate verb.
Identify actual objects and predicative complements accurately.
Form the question or negative with the right auxiliary and plain lexical verb.
alternatives: Accept another defensible answer that meets each stated requirement and preserves the intended meaning.
